The sound Schwa

The most common vowel in English has no name of its own, no letter of its own, and no sound you would call a sound.

The rule

ə

schwa, from Hebrew sva: the void, the nothing.

The most frequent vowel sound in the English language is named after emptiness, because that is what it is: the sound a vowel collapses into when nobody is leaning on it.

Two facts and you have the whole thing:

① The schwa appears only in syllables that are not stressed. Never in a stressed one. So it is not really a vowel you learn, it is what is left when the stress goes elsewhere.

② In French it is roughly the e of demain.

Where the stress is NOT, the vowel goes to nothing.

1 · Any vowel can hide it

This is the part that makes it hard. The schwa is not a letter. All six vowel letters spell it, and the spelling tells you nothing. Tap any word to hear it.

aagain soda Canada
efather problem madness
ipresident family duplicate
ocarrot bottom confirm
usupport circus August
yanalysis pyjamas Pennsylvania

2 · Find the nothing

Say the word out loud. Then click the syllable you threw away.

Word 1 of 0

3 · Your entire component list

In British English, -er and -or endings are /ə/
No r sound. No stress. Nothing.

Which means one rule, learned once, does the entire bench:

resistor capacitor transistor conductor sensor motor transformer inverter converter computer connector parameter amplifier rectifier

4 · But that is not what I hear

Read this before you decide the rule is wrong.

You have heard resistor, sensor and computer a thousand times in games, series and YouTube videos, with a clear, strong r at the end. So this page looks wrong to you.

It is not wrong. You have been listening to Americans.

British English uses /ə/ in words ending -er and -or, while in American English the r is pronounced. American is a rhotic accent: every written r gets said, with the tongue curled back.

Nobody is making a mistake. There are two accents, and your ears have been trained on one of them by everything you watch. That is not a problem, it is an advantage, as long as you know which one you are doing.

What actually sounds odd is switching between the two inside one sentence.

5 · Today's grammar is today's sound

You are learning comparatives this hour. Look at what the comparative ending is.

bigger smaller faster cheaper longer safer

resistor  =  bigger

And the small word nobody says properly: than. In a real comparison it is never said in full. It reduces to /ðən/, and it carries a schwa like everything else that is not important.

This resistor is cheaper than that one.

6 · Say it

Capital letters are stressed: lean on them.

The sensor is connected to a smaller transformer.
This converter is cheaper than that amplifier.
Measure the current, then confirm the value.
-er / -orresistor · capacitor · sensor · motor · computer · converter
comparativesbigger · smaller · faster · cheaper · longer · safer
small wordsa · the · to · of · than · and · was · for (all schwa, all thrown away)
never a schwaany syllable you are leaning on. Stress and schwa cannot share a syllable.
